claims.text: Rapid thermal processing can produce homogeneous, single-phase high-entropy alloy nanoparticles from multimetal precursors.
Rapid thermal processing bypasses diffusion-driven elemental segregation.
Diffusion-driven segregation predominates under slower processing conditions.
The precursor elements are uniformly dispersed at the molecular or nanoparticle level before thermal processing.
Rapid cooling freezes a transient amorphous or metastable mixed state into a homogeneous alloy nanoparticle structure.
Brief thermal exposure reduces the time available for atomic diffusion.
Reduced diffusion time suppresses elemental segregation.
Rapid quenching prevents the system from reaching equilibrium conditions associated with phase separation or decomposition.
Suppressing equilibration ensures a uniform distribution of noble metals.
Rapidly processed nanoparticles will have a uniform elemental distribution.
Rapidly processed nanoparticles will exhibit a single-phase alloy structure.
Rapidly processed nanoparticles will have a lower onset temperature for decomposition than nanoparticles made by the slower baseline process.
The slower baseline treatment permits sufficient atomic diffusion to produce heterogeneity or phase separation.
The proposed mechanism applies to thermally processed noble-metal systems containing five or more elements under inert or controlled atmospheres.
The proposed mechanism may not apply when additives or stabilizers dominate nanoparticle formation.
The proposed mechanism may not apply to synthesis routes that inherently limit cooling rates.
The heating and cooling rate threshold required for complete homogeneity is not established.
Minor local compositional fluctuations may remain undetected by standard characterization methods.

contradictions.description: The mechanism presents rapid processing as preventing decomposition, whereas the predicted outcome assigns the rapidly processed material a lower decomposition onset temperature than the slow-process baseline. These statements are not necessarily logically incompatible because one concerns decomposition during synthesis and the other may concern subsequent thermal analysis, but that distinction is not stated and creates an unresolved tension.
